preview: An interview experience at OFSS covering an online coding round, two technical rounds including DSA and OOPs questions, and a final HR round resulting in selection.
content: Interview Experience Aditya Vivekanand Final Year EXTC (2022-2026) Email: aditya.vivekanand@gmail.com Criteria: 1. CPI: CGPA 7 or equivalent to 70% & above, no standing arrears 2. Class X: 70% and above 3. Class XII: 70% and above 4. Branches: CS, IT, Electrical, EXTC, Electronics. Rounds: 1. Online Coding Round 2. Technical Round – 1 (offline) 3. Technica + HR Round – 2 (offline) 4. HR round (offline) Round 1: Online Coding round (120 mins) It was an online test on the Hackerrank Platform. It consisted of 4 sections Section 1: Medium-Hard Coding Problem. I don’t remember the exact question but it used the concept of Prefix Sum , but on the harder side. Section 2: 20 MCQ on CS core subjects Section 3: 15 MCQ on general aptitude and communication Section 4: Easy Coding Problem. Again, I don’t remember the exact question, but it could be solved easily by sorting and traversing the array, sticking to the given conditions. 46 students were shortlisted. The general tip here is to complete the test with accurate solutions as early as possible because submission timing is also considered in online tests. OFSS had come for roles in 2 businesses: OFSSA and PMD. Shortlisted students were randomly assigned the business to interview in. I was assigned PMD. Round 2: Technical Round (20-25 mins) This round was scheduled on 4th September, 2025. The PPT was presented at 9 a.m., and the interviews began at 11 a.m. Be attentive during the PPT and ask relevant questions—it helps you catch attention. When I was called in, the interviewer greeted me and asked me to sit. The following questions were asked: Tell me about yourself: Frame your answer in such a way that you guide the interviewer toward the topics you want them to ask about. The introduction gives direction to the interviewer and helps them test how well-versed you are with what you’ve mentioned. For example, I wanted to be asked about C++, so I concluded my introduction by mentioning that C++ is my primary programming language. The interviewer then asked whether I knew Java. I told him no. He asked me about the four pillars of OOPs, to give a real-life example of inheritance and explain its usefulness. He further asked me to write the code for multiple inheritance using the example I had given. Next, he asked me about pointers in C++, followed by whether it’s possible to create an object of the base class (in inheritance) and reference it in the derived class. I wasn’t sure of the answer. (Tip: know the ins and outs of anything you mention.) Then, I was asked one basic DSA question: Given an array of size N, return the sum of all 3-digit numbers. Later, he asked me to generalize it to the sum of all K-digit numbers. I solved it in both O(N²) and optimized it to O(N). He seemed satisfied. I was then asked about DBMS and specifically Normalization. It’s best to take a single example and explain all normal forms with that. Since Oracle is a database company, be very thorough with DBMS and SQL. He then asked me about my project, which was based on Reinforcement Learning. Since he wasn’t familiar with RL, I explained the concept, how it differs from ML, and how it was used in my project. Another DSA question followed: For a given number N, determine whether it’s prime or not. I first wrote an O(N) solution, then optimized it to O(√N). I was asked to write both coding questions on paper, and he seemed happy with the solutions. Finally, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about his journey and role at OFSS, as well as the expectations they have from a fresher joining their team. I was called in for the Second Round in 15-20 minutes. But as there were many candidates, my second round was scheduled after the lunch break. Round 3: Technical + HR Round (35-40 mins) My second round was scheduled with the Vice President of the PMD business at OFSS. He began by asking about me, mainly focusing on things that weren’t on my resume. He asked where I was from and what my parents do. Then, he asked about my JEE Mains, JEE Advanced, and MHT-CET scores. He wanted to know why I chose VJTI EXTC instead of taking CS elsewhere. He also asked me about other good colleges in Mumbai and asked me to compare them to VJTI. When he asked whether I had friends in private colleges in Mumbai, I mentioned NMIMS. He noted that Oracle was also recruiting there, and wanted me to compare the pros and cons of the two colleges. He further asked, if I were given the same choices now, which college I would choose. He then asked about the education, curriculum, and professors at VJTI. I was fairly honest in saying that our college has become more of a “historic institution” and has been relatively slow to change. He asked me what essential changes would be needed for VJTI to keep up with the latest academic trends (AI, etc.). (The takeaway here is: feel free to be vocal about your thoughts, but don’t go overboard. The interviewer mainly wanted to gauge how well I communicate and how I think.) After that, he looked at my resume and asked me about my Reinforcement Learning project. I gave him a short explanation of the concept. He asked me how it differs from ML, and then moved on to asking how ChatGPT works. Since I had mentioned LLMs earlier, he also asked me to explain them. He realized I was familiar with these concepts, so he opened the voice assistant on ChatGPT, described a problem statement about how LLMs and RL are used together in the making of ChatGPT, and asked me to debate with it. Here, he essentially wanted to see whether I asked the right questions and countered with the right problems. For example, when GPT started explaining how RL is used over LLMs, I asked: “If we don’t optimize the LLM results with the RL model, what are the better ways to get the desired results?” GPT replied with “better fine-tuning, etc.”, so I followed up with questions about hallucinations and overfitting of data. He seemed quite impressed with the debate and said that he would want to have me on his team. Towards the end, I asked him about his journey to becoming VP. He mentioned that he came from an Electrical background, so I asked him about the challenges he faced when transitioning into a purely Software role and later rising to VP. He spoke for around 7–10 minutes, after which I asked a couple of follow-up questions. Round 4: HR Round Around 3:30 p.m., all the students shortlisted for the HR round in PMD were asked to gather. There were 12 of us. After waiting for about 35–40 minutes, the HR representative entered and announced that all 12 of us had been selected! She asked whether we were all Indian nationals and open to relocating. Finally, she took a group photo with all of us. Tips: Enter with a smile and greet the interviewer—your first impression can make a big impact. Maintain good grooming standards, as they influence your body language and overall presence. Stay calm, composed, and confident—it matters a lot. Prepare your “Tell me about yourself” response and a few common HR questions in advance. Don’t memorize them word-for-word; instead, note key points and frame your answer naturally, since we often forget rehearsed lines under pressure. For DSA questions, think out loud and share your thought process with the interviewer. If the question isn’t clear, don’t hesitate to ask for clarification or request a test case. Once you finish writing your code, dry-run it once. Mirror the interviewer’s energy—smile when they smile, and if they’re serious, stay composed without appearing nervous. Practice mock interviews beforehand—they build confidence and simulate real conditions. While preparing DSA problems, occasionally explain the solution to yourself as if you’re teaching it. In interviews, first present the brute-force solution, then move on to optimizations. Print your resume in color on thick, good-quality paper. It should feel premium when handed to the interviewer. Resources: DSA : Striver SDE Sheet, LeetCode 150 DBMS / SQL : DBMS Gate Smashers, SQL Tutorial, LeetCode SQL 50
